chunks: Al-Husayn ibn ʿUbayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya, from his father, from Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Mahbub, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn, from al-Hasan, from Zurʿa, from Samaʿa, who said:

I asked him about the traveler: how much does he shorten the salat? He said: During a day's journey — and that is two barids, which are eight farsakhs. And whoever travels must shorten the salat and break his fast, except if he is a man accompanying an unjust ruler, or he has gone out for hunting, or he has gone to a village of his own that is a day's journey away while he sleeps [each night returning] to his family — he does not shorten [the prayer] and does not break his fast.

key_terms.الْمُسَافِرِ: the traveler; one who undertakes a legally qualifying journey
key_terms.بَرِيدَانِ: two barids; a barid is a postal-route distance unit (~22 km); two barids is the minimum qasr threshold
key_terms.سُلْطَانٍ جَائِرٍ: an unjust/tyrannical ruler; travel in his company does not qualify for the traveler's dispensations
key_terms.فَرَاسِخَ: farsakhs; plural of farsakh (~5.5 km each); eight farsakhs equals two barids, the minimum travel distance

ai.seo_question: What is the minimum travel distance (in barids and farsakhs) that makes shortening the salat obligatory, according to this hadith from al-Istibsar?
ai.summary: Samaʿa ibn Mihran asks Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) about the minimum travel distance that obligates a traveler to shorten (qasr) the salat. The Imam defines it as a day's journey — two barids or eight farsakhs (approximately 44 km) — and states that any qualifying traveler must shorten the salat and break the obligatory fast. Three exemptions are established where the rulings of travel do not apply: accompanying an unjust ruler, traveling for hunting, and making daily excursions to one's own nearby village while returning home to sleep each night.
